talks.title: What is ATT&CK Coverage, Anyway? | Adam Mashinchi | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Reviews what is ATT&CK Coverage, Anyway? | Adam Mashinchi | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Adam Mashinchi presents at Wild West Hackin' Fest on ATT&CK coverage, completing a trilogy of talks exploring what coverage means and how organizations measure defensive effectiveness.

Key Topics: Defining ATT&CK coverage beyond checkbox compliance; building coverage measurement programs; prior talks at Wild West Hackin' Fest and ATT&CKcon; and practical guidance for spinning up coverage initiatives.

Technical Details: Mashinchi wraps up a three-talk series on ATT&CK coverage, providing updated guidance on measuring which techniques organizations can detect and respond to, moving beyond simply mapping controls to the framework.

Takeaways: ATT&CK coverage requires meaningful measurement of detection and response capability, not just control mapping. Organizations should build programs that validate actual defensive effectiveness.

talks.title: Data is the New Oil | Jeremiah Fowler | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Analyzes data is the New Oil | Jeremiah Fowler | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
From Breach to Research Career

Jeremiah Fowler describes himself as a data hunter, not a deep technical wizard. He entered security after a company data breach while he served as communications and PR director, learning data protection the hard way and later building an internal research center and hiring the researcher who reported the flaw.

Personal Path and Ukraine

His talk weaves career pivots—from Myspace glitter text and a failed music career through subprime-era finance—to moving to Kyiv with his Ukrainian partner. After Russia's invasion, he recounts a four-day wait at the Polish border with his daughter, reflecting on passport privilege amid refugee hardship.

Data as Valuable Asset

Fowler frames exposed data as today's oil: widely sought and routinely mishandled. He cites statistics that nearly 60% of businesses suffered a breach in three years, and argues firms typically invest in security only after an incident—joking that nobody runs a bug bounty until they need one.

Discovery Work in Practice

His Security Discovery work treats open-data hunting as investigative treasure seeking. Examples include railway-station Wi-Fi providers exposing visitor data. The session emphasizes how breach-driven awareness, researcher partnerships, and proactive data exposure hunting can shift organizational priorities.

talks.title: Making the Case for SCA | Alyssa Miller | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Outlines making the Case for SCA | Alyssa Miller | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
From Monoliths to Dependency Trees

Alyssa Miller, business information security officer and former developer, contrasts pre-2004 applications written entirely in-house with modern builds pulling transitive dependencies through Maven, npm, and similar package managers. Developers often cannot enumerate indirect libraries buried deep in dependency graphs.

Landmark Supply-Chain Breaches

Miller revisits Equifax's 2017 breach via an unpatched Apache Struts dependency nested below visible manifests, exposing 164 million consumers. She connects the pattern to Log4j in late 2021—present in 91% of Java apps per Snyk, often as unknown indirect dependencies—and Spring4Shell in 2022, showing the problem accelerating rather than resolved.

The Aviation Weight-and-Balance Analogy

Drawing on her pilot training, Miller compares software composition analysis to aircraft equipment manifests that track every component's weight and position for safe flight. Organizations need analogous visibility into third-party code affecting application center of gravity and risk.

Making the Case for SCA

The talk argues software composition analysis tools, accurate inventories, and developer integration are essential defenses. Without knowing what ships inside binaries, organizations cannot patch, prioritize, or insure against vulnerabilities in code they never wrote but implicitly trust.

talks.title: Security Isn’t What You Do! | Doc Blackburn | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Demonstrates security Isnt What You Do! | Doc Blackburn | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a thought experiment in which the speaker plays a boss asking staff whether the organization is secure. Every yes or no answer is wrong, since nobody can promise a breach will never happen, yet leadership often judges security by whether one occurs. The speaker argues that businesses exist for their mission, so protections that block it get blamed. Examples include a research lab that hid servers from IT and the idea that each protective dollar lowers an asset's value.

Using a hockey analogy, he contrasts defenders, who must cover every route, with attackers, who need only one success and ignore policy and sometimes the law. Breaches are therefore treated as inevitable, and the real task is managing levels of insecurity. Security teams also struggle as a cost center when they do not report the attacks they stop. Randy Martini's advice to never waste a breach is illustrated with a HIPAA enforcement report, which a team can use to ask how it would fare under the same audit.

For practitioners, the first step is changing how they describe their own role, from breach preventers to strategic partners. That means learning the organization's risk appetite, speaking in leadership's language about repeatable processes and dependable results, and reporting the attacks being stopped. The speaker admits he offers no complete fix, since leadership must eventually act.

talks.title: Securing Down Ballot Political Campaigns: The Next Frontier | Daniel Bardenstein | San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Analyzes securing Down Ballot Political Campaigns: The Next Frontier | Daniel Bardenstein | San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Down-ballot threat model

Daniel Bardenstein argues election security discourse focuses on presidential races while state and local campaigns face serious but under-resourced threats. Even small challenger campaigns hold data and infrastructure attackers can disrupt, and every seat affects national governance.

Campaign security gaps

Volunteering for a friend’s congressional primary, he found egregious practices uncommon in enterprise environments: questionable web hosting, limited backend access for defensive scripts, and no budget for professional security tooling. Campaign staff often prioritize fundraising over infrastructure hardening.

DDoS and attribution limits

After DDoS attacks traced to EC2 infrastructure, reporting to authorities yielded little response. Forensics and hardening helped, but the candidate ultimately lost the primary. Bardenstein uses the case to highlight that private citizens and volunteer teams cannot match nation-state or organized troll capabilities alone.

talks.title: Lifting the Veil, a Look at MDE Under the Hood | Olaf Hartong | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Analyzes lifting the Veil, a Look at MDE Under the Hood | Olaf Hartong | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
This talk examines Microsoft Defender for Endpoint as a defender's tool and asks where its telemetry actually comes from. Olaf Hartong walks through the product's parts: the antivirus engine, attack surface reduction rules, exploit protection, application control, and the EDR telemetry that carries most of the value. He notes that an antivirus exclusion does not switch off the other components, so a legitimate binary may need several exclusions, and that the reduction rules can run in audit mode to show what they would have blocked.

The core of the talk covers how the telemetry is produced. Defender relies on a kernel driver that registers callbacks for process, registry, image load and named pipe events, along with many event tracing providers, some of them private to Microsoft. Much of the data is sampled or capped under a configuration that is downloaded from Microsoft and stored locally, and detailed records are kept in the cloud for about 30 days. He compares it with Sysmon, which the user configures and maintains but which only logs, while Defender is fully managed and can isolate machines but gives little control over volume. He also mapped the telemetry onto MITRE ATT&CK data components and found that some Windows audit settings are not enabled by default, so he built a PowerShell script to check Group Policy for them.

The takeaway is to understand what a tool collects, where the data comes from and where its gaps are, since those gaps are often what fails in practice. Defenders should review audit settings, reassess the product regularly because new fields and actions appear with little change documentation, and consider supplementing it with Sysmon or other sources where blind spots matter for detection.

talks.title: Architecting for Ransomware Resilience | Jake Williams | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Presents architecting for Ransomware Resilience | Jake Williams | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that organizations still handle ransomware poorly, and that planning for recovery matters as much as detection. He says standard disaster recovery and business continuity plans were built for natural disasters and non-thinking adversaries, so they fall short when an attacker has already been inside the network. From his incident work, he notes that clients rarely restore everything their backup plan expected.

For backups, he compares offline copies, which are costly and often neglected, with immutable backups, warning that their storage volume must also be locked down. He favors data-only backups restored onto clean systems, trading a tighter recovery point for a longer recovery time. Slow restores from incremental chains and shared storage limits also get attention. On extortion, he says DLP rarely stops data theft, so teams should watch aggregate outbound traffic, flag connections to Mega and rclone executions, and treat living-off-the-land binaries as context-dependent detections. Network segmentation with access control lists is his main lateral movement control, since workstation-to-workstation traffic rarely has a legitimate purpose.

He expects more extortion-only operations, which need less lateral movement, and closes with three principles: layered controls, tested detections that cut through background noise, and a response plan.

talks.title: What Happened to the “Cyber War” Destruction Predictions? | Dave Kennedy | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Details what Happened to the “Cyber War” Destruction Predictions? | Dave Kennedy | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Dave Kennedy, a former military intelligence analyst, addresses why the widely predicted Russian cyber attacks on Ukraine and its allies largely did not materialize. He argues that serious operations against complex organizations and infrastructure need reconnaissance, access and planning, so they cannot be rushed. Ukraine had already been hit repeatedly, including by the 2015 and 2016 outages and NotPetya, and had hardened its defenses, while Starlink kept its command and control running.

He breaks down Russia's services. The GRU is the military-linked unit behind the most destructive operations he cites, including NotPetya, the Black Energy and KillDisk attacks on infrastructure, and interference in the French election. The SVR focuses on long-term intelligence gathering and was linked to the SolarWinds supply chain compromise, while the FSB is mainly domestic. He adds that ransomware groups such as Conti publicly pledged support for Russia and may cause more disruption, with manufacturing among the most frequently hit sectors.

For defenders, he stresses known basics: monitor for unusual behavior and baseline tools like PsExec, PowerShell and WMIC, restrict SMB, RPC and workstation-to-workstation traffic, remove administrator rights from users, and run purple-team exercises. He flags supply chain trust and cloud visibility as priority risks, and concludes that ransomware is the greater near-term threat for most organizations than a sweeping nation-state cyber war.

talks.title: What rattles around in the mind of your CISO? | Russell Eubanks | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Examines what rattles around in the mind of your CISO? | Russell Eubanks | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at Wild West Hackin' Fest San Diego 2022, Russell Eubanks—former Senior Vice President, CIO, and CISO of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta—shares insights into executive leadership and the mindset of a Chief Information Security Officer. Reflecting on his career journey from working manual labor in a Maytag factory to executive leadership and ultimately starting his own consulting business on March 9, 2020, Eubanks emphasizes the core principle of getting wisdom as cheaply as possible by learning from others. He breaks down the responsibilities rattling around in a CISO's mind into three core leadership dimensions: leading up, leading down, and leading laterally.

### Key Topics
- **Leading Up (Speaking the Language of Business):** Eubanks distinguishes between being managed and actively leading up. To communicate effectively with executive leadership, boards, and CFOs, security leaders must translate technical data into business impact. Using Nordstrom's mission statement ("to give customers the most compelling shopping experience possible") as an illustration, he emphasizes that security tasks (e.g., log reviews, policy compliance, incident response) must explicitly tie back to why the organization exists rather than existing for cybersecurity's sake alone.
- **Leading Down (Mentoring, Vision, and Strategic Accountability):** Leaders must transition from hands-on technical execution to verbs like leading, motivating, sharing, and succession planning. Eubanks highlights the necessity of grooming successors (sharing his experience mentoring Alan to take over as CISO at the Atlanta Fed) and establishing clear strategic roadmaps. He also stresses identifying "what can only you do" each day, prioritizing high-leverage responsibilities that unblock teams.
- **Leading Laterally (Peer Alignment and Actionable Security):** Working across the organization with non-technical peers (such as financial or facilities leaders) requires making cybersecurity relevant without overwhelming them. Rather than relying on vague platitudes like "cyber is everyone's job," leaders should give colleagues clear, simple calls to action (e.g., specific channels to report anomalies). Furthermore, security leaders must balance their calendar time between internal security team operations and peer engagement across the wider organization.

### Technical Details
- **Detecting Authorized vs. Unauthorized Change:** Eubanks introduces a framing question for technical stakeholders: *"How long can you stand to not know?"* For example, asking network administrators how long they can tolerate not knowing when a production firewall running configuration has changed (e.g., 5 minutes), or asking Windows administrators when an account is added to Domain Admins. Security operations can then implement configuration monitoring and log analysis tied into change management systems to differentiate authorized ticketed maintenance windows from unapproved changes.
- **CISO Mind Map:** Attribution is given to Rafeeq's CISO Mind Map as a structured reference categorizing executive security responsibilities, spanning business alignment, budget, governance, policy, and strategic planning.

### Takeaways
- Align daily cybersecurity tasks directly with organizational mission statements so business executives understand funding and operational value.
- Security leaders should hold themselves accountable daily to high-impact tasks that only they can accomplish, such as board briefings, succession planning, and resource approvals.
- Help peer leaders and employees take security with them by providing actionable, singular reporting instructions rather than generic slogans.
- Maintain an intentional balance on the calendar between internal departmental support and cross-functional organizational relationship-building.

talks.title: Hacking my Bank with OSINT | Matthew Toussain | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Presents hacking enterprise Bank with OSINT | Matthew Toussain | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through an end-to-end open-source intelligence workflow aimed at one person, with the speaker using his own accounts as the target. Starting from a seed such as a name, username, domain or IP address, it pivots through registries, search engines, reverse image search and people-search sites to build a profile. It shows how login error messages can confirm whether an email address exists, and how the Mail Sniper tool automates that check against Microsoft and Google Workspace.

The middle section turns collected data into access. Breach compilations supply passwords for credential stuffing, and full breach records can also expose addresses and Social Security numbers. Public voter records provide home addresses, and support staff and security questions offer another route in. An incident response case about an insider who sent unauthorized patient text messages shows how the same techniques helped with attribution.

The closing part covers recovery and multi-factor gaps. A bank that silently truncated passwords to 12 characters shows how a rule meant to cut help-desk calls weakens login. A Google sign-in response code revealed accounts without two-factor enrollment despite an organization's policy. The practical takeaway is to run these checks against your own exposure, treat account recovery and MFA enrollment as attack surface, and assume personal details already sit in public breach data.

talks.title: Move in Silence: Staying Quiet in Mature Networks | Cory Wolff | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Investigates move in Silence: Staying Quiet in Mature Networks | Cory Wolff | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that red teamers working in mature enterprises, with SOCs, incident response teams and EDR, can't rely on noisy scanners without being noticed. The speaker presents a quiet reconnaissance methodology built on three questions: where the attacker is, where the domain controller sits, and where the member servers are. Simple steps come first. These include reading the ARP table, sending a broadcast ping that may expose legacy hosts, packet captures filtered by service, and treating the DHCP-assigned DNS server as a likely domain controller. Checking environment variables is preferred over running commands like whoami, which endpoint tools flag.

The middle of the talk covers Active Directory discovery. Dumping LDAP with an anonymous bind, where it is allowed, returns computers, users and groups in a single query, which the speaker prefers to BloodHound because BloodHound contacts each host. Reverse DNS lookups on the hostnames can then build an IP list. Self-signed certificate issuers can reveal internal AD CS deployments and device types. SMB signing status helps pick relay targets, and the speaker notes that domain controllers and newer member servers usually require signing. Other points include avoiding Mimikatz in favour of process-based LSASS dumps, using mTLS command channels, SSL tunnels and DNS over HTTPS, and being wary of PowerShell and C# because the CLR makes them easier to monitor.

The closing takeaway is that patience and restraint matter more than tooling. If ICMP sweeps are blocked, the speaker falls back to checking for a single expected open port on each host. In the Q&A, he notes that firewalls such as Cisco ASAs can break under half-open scan traffic, so full TCP scans are sometimes needed instead.

talks.title: Hiding in plain sight from blue teams | Henri Hambartsumyan | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Demonstrates hiding in plain sight from blue teams | Henri Hambartsumyan | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Henri Hambartsumyan, who does purple teaming, argues that many detection rules depend on filters that exclude legitimate software known to behave oddly. Blue teams usually allowlist those applications after triage, and that creates a predictable gap. Rather than killing or bypassing the EDR, an operator can imitate an application that is already trusted and slip past the filters. He notes this is especially useful during initial access, when an attacker has a macro-enabled document but no elevated privileges.

The middle of the talk walks through data from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and attack surface reduction rules. Examples include Excel add-in files that load often in large environments, Office processes that routinely spawn child processes, a common run-dll call tied to a printer driver, and process names that constantly read LSASS memory. He also shows that process injection using the common remote-thread API is so widespread among vendor software that the rarer APIs can make an operator stand out more. Decompiled attack surface reduction exclusion lists and a Defender configuration filter keyed on a binary's original file name and signing level are discussed as further examples of the same weakness.

The closing advice is aimed at defenders. Match full file paths instead of bare file names, assume attackers know your filters, build redundant detections for the same behavior, and review accumulated exclusions periodically. Overly complex rules become hard to maintain, so a balance is needed. The speaker withheld the full exclusion lists from publication.

talks.title: The Invisibility Cloak: Obfuscate C# Tools to Evade Signature Based Detection | Brett Hawkins
talks.teaser: See how changing tool strings and identifiers can bypass some detections, and where those changes still fall short.
talks.summary: The speaker demonstrates how Invisibility Cloak changes C# tools’ names, project identifiers, debug strings and string values to evade signature based detection. Through demos with several tools, attendees see which detections these changes bypass, where method or variable names still trigger detection, and how disabling AMSI offers another way to run tools in memory. The talk also covers defensive steps, including keeping host security products updated and focusing detection on techniques rather than tool names.

talks.title: Vulnerability analysis: most likely doing it wrong | John Strand & Bryson Bort | San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Analyzes vulnerability analysis: most likely doing it wrong | John Strand & Bryson Bort | San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a defense of deception technology. The speakers argue that tripwires such as honey accounts, Kerberoastable accounts and planted files are worth the cost because they alert defenders and make attackers slow down to judge whether a system is watched. They then separate adversary simulation, which approximates one step such as encrypting dummy files on a single host, from adversary emulation, which follows the whole chain through command and control and data exfiltration. Atomic Red Team is presented as useful but limited, since its tests run in isolation rather than as a connected attack path.

Using MITRE ATT&CK as a periodic table, the speakers argue that attacks are state-based chains and that most techniques in new campaigns repeat older ones, so testing chains matters more than chasing single indicators. They criticize threat intelligence feeds of stale hashes and IP addresses, noting that changing one byte defeats a file hash. They also argue that vulnerability scanners rarely surface post-exploitation paths, that phishing metrics can mislead, and that restricting access to uncategorized domains can reduce exposure more than repeated awareness training.

The closing discussion covers the limits of EDR and red team engagements, which are only snapshots in time, and the difficulty of segmenting or air-gapping legacy and operational technology networks. The practical takeaways are to map defenses against end-to-end attack paths, treat risk as something to mitigate rather than eliminate, and assign clear ownership of assets and remediation with executive backing.

talks.title: Hacking Azure services for bounties and credentials | Josh Magri | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Provides hacking Azure services for bounties and credentials | Josh Magri | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that Azure is a rich target because much of the platform is abstracted away from users, and a flaw in a shared service can expose every customer that relies on it. The speaker lays out the Azure hierarchy of tenants, management groups, subscriptions and resource groups, and the roles that can be assigned at each scope, including owner, contributor, reader and user access administrator. The distinction is drawn between provider-side exploits, which get fixed, and abuses of intended features, which often do not.

The middle of the talk covers several cases. In Logic Apps, an API connection created for one action could be reused for other actions the user could reach, so a reader-level principal could list and read Key Vault secrets in another resource group. Inspecting traffic revealed an undocumented dynamic invoke endpoint that exposed subscriptions outside the user's scope, and a path traversal in the resource group field allowed a role assignment at subscription level; Microsoft fixed that one. In Azure Automation, hybrid workers exposed automation account keys and secrets to readers, letting an attacker register a machine and pull certificates and credentials. A related leak put private keys into service principal manifests, readable by reader-level users in Azure AD. The talk also covers smaller items such as secrets in VM extension settings, policy definitions, function app file systems, and a predictable prefix in service principal secrets that helps locate and validate credentials.

The closing guidance is practical: use managed identities instead of stored credentials, model the tenant as a graph to spot dangerous paths, and regularly audit and revoke access that is no longer needed.
